Texts Show Kimberly Guilfoyle Seeking $100,000 and Offering Access to Trump Officials
 
Plus, rogue pilots are now one of the biggest threats to airline safety—and the race is on for next summer’s $50,000 internships
 
 
NATHAN HOWARD/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Kimberly Guilfoyle was preparing for her congressional hearing to become U.S. ambassador to Greece when she reached out to a Trump donor with an urgent request: She needed $100,000 that she said she owed American Express—in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail.

 

The MAGA ally didn’t ultimately make the payment. But the back and forth, part of a tranche of hundreds of messages, emails and letters reviewed by the Journal, raises new questions about one of America’s most high-profile ambassadors.

 

Last week, Guilfoyle came under fire from Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees, who urged the State Department to review her conduct. They cited our previous investigation into her promotion of a Greek company whose lobbyist traveled with her to meetings with governments.

 

Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, said the ambassador disputed the authenticity of the messages but declined to provide specifics.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Democrats expect to win the House. Here’s their to-do list.

 

• Three fired OpenAI employees called on the company to work with outside safety auditors and to preserve the ability to monitor artificial-intelligence models.

 

• Oracle, Broadcom and SpaceX are seeking blockbuster debt deals to pay for AI chips.

 

• Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is betting his left-wing coalition can avoid a bruising election defeat amid outrage over the eviction of an elderly woman who died Wednesday.

 

• A spy crisis is threatening to defang Germany’s top intelligence agency—and the timing is disastrous for Berlin, which wants to expand the agency’s powers to counter threats from Russia.

 

• Attacks claimed by Houthi militants damaged two airports in Saudi Arabia, including one in its capital, killing three people and wounding 36 others.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Rogue pilots have become one of the biggest threats to airline safety.

 

A pilot’s suspected attempt to crash a passenger jet bound for Israel shows how one of aviation’s biggest safety threats is in the cockpit. As commercial flying has got safer, the death toll from suspected intentional crashes increasingly stands out, reports Andrew Tangel. At least 800 people worldwide have died since 2005 in airline crashes that U.S. government officials have suspected or confirmed were intentionally caused by pilots, according to accident data. But aviation security and safety experts say advances in training and modern airliners’ technological safeguards can only do so much when screening for potential rogue pilots falls short.

 

5.

 

Erling Haaland conquered the world’s biggest sport. Then he came for America.

 

When the soccer player first touched down in the U.S. for the World Cup, he was best known to the rest of the world as an icy goal machine. By the time he left, he was the viral Norseman who’d set the tournament ablaze, scoring seven goals in five matches at a faster clip than Lionel Messi. Although Norway didn’t win the trophy, it’s safe to say that no one had a better time. As Haaland put it, the visit to America became the ultimate “lads’ trip.” It also just happened to turn into a cross-cultural love fest. Joshua Robinson caught up with Norway’s 6-foot-5 striker on terrifying his opponents—and the surreal World Cup summer that turned him into much more than a soccer star.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Here’s what six years of inflation mean for the midterms.

 
 
.
 

Four years ago, in the run-up to the last midterm elections, prices were rising more than twice as quickly as they are now. President Trump has repeatedly reminded voters of the 2022 inflation rate, blaming high prices on his predecessor. But Americans, weary from six years of steepening prices that have eaten away at their paychecks, might blame Republicans anyway as they head to the polls next month.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

• Earnings: PepsiCo

8. THE NUMBER

 
$50,000
 

The compensation that elite financial firms are dangling for 10-week summer internships. Outfits such as Citadel and Jane Street are hustling to lock down the most promising talent before their rivals do. Some students already have offers for 2027 or are deep in the interview process. In this arms race, 20-year-olds now command pay rates that most Americans don’t reach at the peaks of their careers.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

An army of ‘phone spotters’ is racing against the clock to save rural pay phones, 52 calls at a time.

 

William Arnold drove 900 miles from his home in Cornwall, England, this summer to a windswept pay phone on the Isle of Lewis in Scotland. When he got there, he pulled out a big bag of coins and started making calls, 52 of them to be precise. In doing so, he ensured the phone booth met the minimum threshold of a call a week to stay in service for another year. He also inspired others, driven by nostalgia—and maybe the apocalypse—to do their bit to save the last of the U.K.’s public pay phones.
